body: Errors can now also have Code Actions associated with them. For now, this is just utilized so that warnings *treated as errors* can still have their Code Actions appear, but I don't think anything's preventing error-specific Code Actions.

Some improvements:

- Quick Fixes are now grouped in the menu by the warning they're addressing.
- Pressing Alt + Enter in the editor brings up the menu.
- A whole bunch more warnings have Quick Fixes:
  - UNUSED_PRIVATE_CLASS_VARIABLE
  - UNTYPED_DECLARATION
  - INFERRED_DECLARATION
  - UNUSED_LOCAL_CONSTANT
  - ASSERT_ALWAYS_TRUE
  - REDUNDANT_AWAIT
  - STATIC_CALLED_ON_INSTANCE
  - MISSING_AWAIT
  - INT_AS_ENUM_WITHOUT_CAST

Unfortunately I've run into what feels like an impasse at the moment. At the point in the analyzer where warnings are pushed, information about the indentation level of the statements seems to have been lost. This makes it difficult to implement code actions that insert text at the same indentation level as the line with the warning, because if a warning is being emitted from a sub-part of the line, we don't know where to insert the new text. Addressing this will likely require storing additional data in the parser/tokenizer nodes. If anyone has better or more efficient ideas on how to approach this, please let me know!

The GDScriptParser now gives each node a pointer to its parent suite when `TOOLS_ENABLED` is set. This way, we can access any node's suite, and from that determine the correct indentation to place new code at. Unfortunately, it seems to be broken with inner classes at the moment, as they are not parsed as suites...

Inner classes are not suites. A suite is a collection of executable code statements (e.g. function body).

The term you are looking for might be scopes. But I don't think there is any construct like that in the GDScript stack. A more generalized parent pointer in the AST might make more sense.

That was what I understood from experimenting with it, so it's great to hear it confirmed!

A parent pointer could be the best option in the long run; I thought it might also be possible to store both the suite and class for each node, or `nullptr` if there is none. The system would first check for a suite, and use its indentation if it exists; if not, it would check the class, and if that also (somehow?) didn't exist, it would assume zero indentation.

Again though, if aiming to make these additions to the parser more useful for other applications in addition to this specific one, just allowing nodes to know their "parent" might be more useful.

I've made a lot of progress on this! Code Actions now support the LSP. This means that they can be activated from an external editor like VS Code!

In designing this to support the LSP, document edits can now be performed across multiple files simultaneously. This opens the door for other refactoring operations, such as renaming symbols, to be easily implemented using this system.

There is a bit of a difficult point I've run into during this process. Currently, running a multi-document edit operation (such as a Code Action) doesn't apply to the undo/redo stack. It simply opens each file and performs the necessary edits. I think having the ability to undo and redo these multi-document edits will be important; I've found myself attempting to Cmd+Z away a Code Action many times just while testing. Is it standard or acceptable to have a single undo/redo action change the contents of multiple files at once like this?

I've also got to figure out how to properly handle columns and tab characters. Godot seems to treat a tab character as the number of columns specified in the editor settings, so some conversions will be necessary there to get things correctly aligned.

Thanks for the videos and info! I believe this is the columns-vs-tab-characters problem discussed above; the GDScript parser counts the right side of a single tab character as column 4, while the text editor counts it as just a single character `\t`. So, when the code action says "insert `@warning_ignore` at column 4", the text editor goes to what it considers column/position 4 within the line, which is right after `\tvar`.

To support this hypothesis, I think if you configure the editor to use spaces instead of tabs, and then reformat your script to correspond, it *should* line up correctly. Getting this conversion figured out is my main priority for this PR.

Your suggestion of the downwards caret indicator is a good one, and something I've been hoping to suggest for other dropdown menu buttons in the editor. If we go that route, I'm not sure if I should try to draw the caret from its own icon on top of the lightbulb icon, or if I should just update the lightbulb icon to include the caret in it. I'm currently leaning towards the former at least for now, and will try to give it a shot soon! --- > This seems like a bug. Adding the underscore in front of this variable doesn't fix it. Looks like this is technically expected behavior. There are two warnings there: one for `UNTYPED_DECLARATION` and one for `UNUSED_VARIABLE`. When you add the underscore, it takes care of the `UNUSED_VARIABLE` warning. The `UNTYPED_DECLARATION` one remains, so the line keeps the yellow highlight and the code action to add the `@warning_ignore` for `UNTYPED_DECLARATION` makes the lightbulb button stay there. If you clicked the lightbulb a second time, it should just suggest you ignore the remaining warning, and after that it would disappear. I recognize the in-editor communication on this isn't great though 😅 In [KoBeWi's clips here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/114168#issuecomment-3873567286) you can see that for a period of time, the in-editor code actions were categorized by the warnings they addressed. I ended up removing that because it didn't align well with how the LSP/VS Code provided code actions, and also made the code for detecting a particular code action's selection a bit more complicated. This is perhaps something where the editor itself could use some work beyond this PR, indicating how many warnings on a single line there are. So once you fix _one_ of the warnings, you'd get instant feedback that something has changed (i.e., there are fewer warnings left to fix). --- > Just from a graphic design standpoint, I feel like the floating window with the fix options needs a header (greyed out a bit). VSCode gives it a header too. Maybe something generic like 'Fix warning'? IIRC VS Code it labels it simply as "Quick Fix", which makes sense for warnings and errors as well as other potential actions that people may want to introduce in the future. I can try adding a header line to the dropdown like that 🙂

Just a thought, but I think it would be nice to: - Order the options alphabetically or by type; the scattering of 'Ignores' looks a bit weird here: - Offer a 'fix all' option, I believe Rider and VSCode do this too. That should probably be in a separate, later PR though, since that would require deciding priority between the actions, e.g. whether to remove the unused variable or add the underscore. An alternative would be to mimick Rider's quick-fix menu, which has each Menu Item fold out a side menu, so you can choose one of the main options, then fold out a menu to select 'Fix all in function / Fix all in file / Fix all in project'

> [I think it would be nice to] Order the options alphabetically or by type

Technically they are being ordered here, by the warnings they're addressing. There are two warnings on the line in that screenshot. The first is `UNTYPED_DECLARATION` and has no special code actions associated with it, only the default "ignore" action. The second is `UNUSED_VARIABLE` and has two code actions as well as its corresponding "ignore" action. (The "ignore" action always comes last in the list for each warning.)

So, if we were to add an "Add type for this declaration" action for `UNTYPED_DECLARATION`, the list would look like:
- Add type for this declaration
- Ignore "UNTYPED_DECLARATION"
- Add underscore to variable name
- Remove variable declaration
- Ignore "UNUSED_VARIABLE"

For a period of time, the list in Godot provided section headers for each warning, which made it clearer. However, since there wasn't LSP support for this (as far as I could see), I ended up removing it to keep things simple and unified.

I don't know off-hand how to set up a scenario in VS Code with some other language server, where it would suggest me code actions to fix multiple warnings/errors on the same line. But if we were able to come up with such a scenario, we could see how they handle it.

> Offer a 'fix all' option

This does sound like a neat idea! I'd have to investigate more how this works, but looking at the [code action LSP page](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#codeAction), it sounds like marking a particular code action as preferred would be a simple matter of sending the `isPreferred` property as true. Integrating it into the built-in editor might be a little bit more work, but presumably not too much.

Still though, as you said, we'd have to decide for each warning which code actions should be considered "preferred" on top of implementing the editor and LSP functionality, so I think it would be best as a follow-up.

I looked a bit more into the possibility of moving the code action functionality from CodeEdit to CodeTextEditor this evening, and (so far) I don't think it would make sense. Functionality like the icon and tooltip is tied to methods in CodeEdit itself, so accessing those from CodeTextEditor would require work on CodeEdit/TextEdit.

I suppose I could give a shot at another approach to displaying the code actions button, where instead of custom-drawing the icon I just use a Button node that I reposition at the correct location. If that works well, then CodeTextEdit may be able to handle all the logic and leave CodeEdit relatively untouched. But otherwise, at the moment I think the best thing might just be to keep most of the code as-is in CodeEdit, and un-expose things like `document_edits_requested`, *or* work on exposing the whole code actions workflow through CodeEdit so that it can be used by others.

The icon itself needs to be moved out since I don't think there can be private theme icons, it should be possible to get it in `CodeTextEditor::_update_text_editor_theme`.
For drawing it you can connect to the draw signal and use the same `get_text_canvas_item` CI. For drawing over line numbers (if it is kept) it could draw a backround behind it and just draw on top of the number instead.
The tooltip on the icon, can be triggered in `CodeTextEditor::_text_editor_gui_input`.
If that isn't working it can be a separate button, though it should be clipped somehow (probably).
I don't think I saw anything that can't be done outside of CodeEdit, but we can make more methods public if needed for it.

And for the vertical position, try to use the `get_rect_at_line_column` instead of `get_caret_draw_pos`, since the draw pos one has some additional vertical offset.

The behavior shown below is IMO confusing / unexpected, and stopping me from approving this PR from a usability point of view.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/52e177a6-80ef-4310-9824-34a848da7368

In short, the dropdown currently has options that don't apply to the line on which the fix icon was clicked. In my example, both dropdowns spawned by clicking lines 4 and 5 contain the "add underscore to name" and "ignore 'UNUSED_PARAMETER'" options that should only apply to line 3. Subsequently, and compounding the confusion, picking those options doesn't actually fix anything on those lines! And to compound even more confusion, when the 'add underscore' option to line 5 (turning the line into `var _yo`) is applied, the valid fix of removing the unused variable is also no longer present.

All of the behavior shown in the video looks correct to me.

The lines shown have the following warnings:
- Line 3 has `UNUSED_PARAMETER` (`delta` is never used)
- Line 4 has `UNTYPED_DECLARATION` (the type of `hello` is not specified) and `UNUSED_VARIABLE` (`hello` is never used)
- Line 4 has `UNTYPED_DECLARATION` (the type of `yo` is not specified) and `UNUSED_VARIABLE` (`yo` is never used)

When you select line 3, you have the option to "Add underscore to *parameter* name"; the parameter is the `delta` parameter to `_process`.
When you select lines 4 or 5, you have the option to "Add underscore to *variable* name"; the variable here is `hello` or `yo` for line 4 and 5 respectively (depending on which line you have selected and are applying the action to).

After applying the "add underscore" action to line 5, the `UNUSED_VARIABLE` warning is no longer present since the analyzer doesn't apply it when a variable name starts with an underscore. It takes the leading underscore to mean that the user is aware the variable is unused and is okay with that. Since the warning is no longer there, the code actions associated with the warning aren't either.

Later on, we could potentially add code actions that become available separate from warnings, including one that suggests removing unused variables whose names start with underscores. That would expand the scope of this PR beyond what I'd like to do at the moment though, so it would be best to come in a follow-up after discussion about if it's ultimately necessary.

---

To improve the issue with the "Add underscore to parameter/variable name" issue, I suppose we could add the identifier's name to the message itself, so it says something like

or

> Add underscore to variable name "hello"

making it more clear which identifier is going to be modified by the code action.

> Do any of the current Code Actions work on multiple documents at once? If none of the current actions need it could be done later.

To the best of my memory, and from skimming the changes, no current code actions work on multiple documents at once. However, the format for storing code action information defined by the LSP (which I've tried to preserve as much as possible for the internal Godot implementation) _does_ allow for edits to multiple documents to be specified as part of the overall code action operation.

The current code for performing the document edits (including multiple documents at once, if it is passed such an edit request) can be found at [`ScriptEditor::_on_document_edits_requested()`](https://github.com/Meorge/godot/blob/f6edc05ed534ba7c9505a5a30acca05edff1c591/editor/script/script_editor_plugin.cpp#L3780). It opens a script editor for every document that's part of the overall edit operation, then performs all of the edits for each document in the corresponding editor.

For now, since no multi-document code actions are defined, I suppose we could hardcode Godot to only perform the edits for the first (and only) document in the operation. Then once we have multi-document edit operations, we can do a follow-up PR that implements a more robust system like the one you described. If we did this, we could also add a warning/error message to the `_on_document_edits_requested()` method that triggers if a multi-document edit is attempted. While I think the current implementation would work "well enough" for multi-document edits, it hasn't been tested for that. So I wouldn't want someone to try implementing one and assuming it would definitely work 😅
